newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels release two hostages despite defiance.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels release two hostages despite defiance.

text.p: Marxist rebels freed two more hostages on Tuesday -- leaving 81 inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's home in Lima -- after an early show of defiance that crushed hopes for a quick end to the two-week-old crisis.
Honduran ambassador Jose Eduardo Martell Mejia and Argentine consul general Juan Ibanez were released from the residence at about 5 p.m. local time (2200 GMT).
Dressed in suits and carrying plastic bags with personal belongings, the two men appeared in good health as they walked out and hugged Red Cross officials before being driven away in a police car.
The remaining hostages included the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, dozens of Japanese businessmen and most of the top officials of Peru's police and intelligence forces.
The releases followed a carefully-staged propaganda coup by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) that shattered hopes the crisis might end by New Year.
From around 10 a.m. local time (1500 GMT), the rebels invited journalists camped in the streets outside to witness firsthand conditions inside the residence and to hear a series of militant messages.

MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini -- dressed in green military fatigues and covering his face with a red-and-white handkerchief -- said the rebels would not modify their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
"We are inflexible in our original position," Cerpa said from within the building. "I do not see an immediate solution," he added, insiting the rebels were in "no hurry" to end the standoff.
The MRTA head said, however, that the group had left "the doors open" and was "open to any mediator ... (Cuban leader Fidel) Castro or (Russian President) Boris Yeltsin or whoever."
The rebels paraded their key hostage, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, in front of reporters. A relaxed- looking Tudela called for a peaceful solution to the crisis.
Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail party stormed two weeks ago by the rebels, was also brought before the cameras.
Looking grave and tired he offered apologies for the embassy's involvement in the crisis. "A thousand apologies from my government," he said in faltering Spanish.

In a brief walkie-talkie interview with Reuters, Cerpa said the MRTA had already achieved its aim of drawing world attention to the bad conditions of Peruvian jails, and would now concentrate on obtaining the release of prisoners.
He said responsibility for resolving the crisis lay with the government. "There has been no opening up. This is now in the hands of the government. The government must reflect," Cerpa said.

He and about four other rebels wering combat gear and with ammunition strapped to their bodies met the group of about a dozen cameramen and photographers allowed inside the building for the first time since the crisis began.
Reuters photographer Zoraida Diaz, among the group, said the rebels spoke calmly, insisted they were not terrorists and repeated demands for improved jail conditions for comrades.
Diaz said furniture was pushed up against windows inside the building as a barricade.

The Red Cross, apparently unhappy that journalists were allowed into the mined and booby-trapped compound, withdrew temporarily from the site but returned by mid-afternoon to take food and provisions into the residence.

Tuesday's burst of activity followed public expressions of hope from both Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and his Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi that the crisis would be brought to a peaceful end.
But their tone was quickly undermined by Cerpa's comments and an earlier statement shouted by an unidentified rebel to the first group of reporters who approached the building.
The rebel slammed Fujimori's government as a "dictatorship dressed up as a democracy" and practicing "state terrorism that kills through starvation."

He shouted that the guerrillas were "determined to make the ultimate sacrifice" in the siege. "Any harm to them (the remaining hostages) will be the exclusive responsibility of the government of Mr. Fujimori if he decides upon a military intervention."

The rebels' defiant tone contrasted with the more conciliatory statement they issued at the weekend after the release of 20 hostages and a first face-to-face meeting between the guerrillas and government negotiator Domingo Palermo.

In an interview with the Spanish news agency Efe made available to Reuters, Fujimori said earlier on Tuesday the crisis could be resolved without violence but insisted the guerrillas lay down their arms and free all their captives.
"I believe that in the end reason will impose a solution without the spilling of blood, fully respectful of the human rights of the hostages and hostage-takers," he said.

Fujimori said he would not free any MRTA members from Peru's prisons. He said that if his government was to rule out the use of force, the rebels must put down their weapons and free the hostages to a "commission of guarantors".

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was confident of the Peruvian government's ability to handle the crisis -- so much so that he was going ahead with a five-nation Asian trip next week that officials had earlier said might be cancelled.
